I had a job interview downtown, and I planned everything perfectly the night before.
New shirt, printed resume, left the house early so I definitely wouldn't be late.
The sky looked a little gray that morning, but the forecast said light clouds, nothing serious at all.
I trusted it completely, which was mistake number one.
I decided to walk instead of taking a cab, since the office was only about fifteen minutes away and I wanted the fresh air to calm my nerves before the interview.
About halfway there, the wind picked up out of nowhere, and the sky went from gray to almost black in what felt like two minutes flat.
Then it just opened up.
Not a light drizzle, not a normal rain, but the kind of storm where you can barely see the street in front of you.
I didn't have an umbrella, obviously, because the forecast had completely lied to me, so I just started running, holding my folder over my head like that was somehow going to help.
By the time I reached the building, I was completely soaked from head to toe.
My shirt was stuck to me, my resume was basically wet paper, and my shoes were making a squishing sound with every single step I took.
I stood in the lobby dripping onto the marble floor, watching a small puddle slowly form around my feet.
The receptionist looked at me, then handed me a stack of paper towels without saying a single word, like this happens all the time around there.
Another woman waiting in the lobby gave me a sympathetic little smile, the kind that said she'd probably been there before too.
I did my best to dry off in the bathroom, but honestly, there's only so much you can do with paper towels and a hand dryer.
My hair had basically given up entirely, and my resume looked like it had survived a small flood, but there was no time left to fix any of that properly.
I walked into the interview still a little damp, and honestly, still a little embarrassed about the whole situation.
But instead of pretending everything was fine, I just told them exactly what happened, storm and all.
The interviewer actually laughed and said it was the most memorable entrance anyone had made all year.
I got the job about a week later, and my new manager told me on my first day that half the office already knew the story before I'd even started.
Turns out, showing up looking like a wet dog and being completely honest about it made a much better impression than a perfectly dry, boring interview ever could have.
